         September 2026 Article 405 Deviation Reporting Response to Comment of

Dear Secretary Reese,

On October 9, 2026, Kleinschmidt Associates, on behalf of C-S Canal Hydro LLC, operator and
licensee for the Waterloo and Seneca Falls Project (FERC No. 2438) on the Seneca River in
New York, submitted the License Article 405 Deviation Report (Report) for the month of
September. On October 15, 2026, William H. Roege submitted comments on the Report
identifying discrepancies in the data. By letter dated October 23, 2026, the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (FERC) required a response to William H. Roege’s comments within
15 days (November 7, 2026). Responses to those comments are provided herein in
Attachment A.

In addition to the comment responses below, the Report has been revised to correct the
identified discrepancies and offer clarification where needed. The Report is available in
Attachment B. The data spreadsheets for the months of July, August, and September have
also been corrected and are provided in their Excel format in addition to this response
document.

Please contact me at Sydney.Robinson@Kleinschmidtgroup.com or Kelly Maloney at
Kelly.maloney@relevatepower.com if you have any questions or require additional
information regarding this matter.

Sincerely,

KLEINSCHMIDT ASSOCIATES

   ATTACHMENT A

COMMENT RESPONSES
                                     Responses to Comments


Comment 1

September precipitation explanation

The report states that September precipitation was approximately 25 percent of normal and
identifies abnormally low precipitation as the cause of the continuing deviation from the licensed
lake elevation.

However, Figure 6 in Attachment C depicts precipitation for September 28 through October 4,
rather than the September 1–30 reporting period. The Northeast Regional Climate Center's
(NRCC) precipitation map for September 1–30 indicates that precipitation across the Seneca Lake
watershed was near normal. (see attachment).

Furthermore, the report's own Geneva precipitation information indicates approximately five
inches of rainfall during September, compared with the historical average September precipitation
of 3.39 inches.

We request that FERC require the licensee to correct or substantiate their precipitation statement
and reassess its explanation for the continuing lake-level deviation.


       Response:

       The figure in Attachment C was mistakenly included with the incorrect dates, and used as
       a reference in the explanation for why the Seneca Lake levels are in deviation. The Report
       has been revised to include a figure with the correct date range of September 1 through
       September 30. The updated figure (Figure 1) shows that precipitation was between 75 to
       125% of normal in the area of the Seneca Falls and Waterloo dam drainage areas, rather
       than the incorrectly reported 25% in the initial September Report. Figure 2 depicts the
       percent of normal precipitation for the area between July 1, 2026 and September 30, 2026,
       and shows that the precipitation within the area of the Project during the three months
       preceding the September Report was also below average. The average precipitation total
       (1991-2020) for the months of July and September in the Climate Region 10 – Central
       Lakes, which includes the Seneca Falls and Waterloo Project is 4 inches. While the average
       precipitation total for the area in August is 2.2 inches. The total precipitation for September
       is shown in Figure 3 and the total precipitation from July 1, 2026 to September 30, 2026 is
       shown in Figure 4.

       A significant portion of inflows into Seneca Lake are provided via Keuka Lake at its outlet
       in Dresden, NY. The Keuka Lake USGS Gage 04232482 shown in Figure 5 demonstrates
       that releases from the lake outlet have generally been consistently under 25 cfs.
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
November 9, 2026                                                                                   5.


         Although the precipitation reported in the September Report was incorrect, the small
         increase in precipitation for the region was still generally below average for this time of
         year, and July through September tends to be relatively dry in terms of total precipitation.
         The below average precipitation levels for the summer and into the fall of 2026 remains
         accurate as the cause of the lake level deviation.

Comment 2

Van Cleef Lake operating elevation

The May 2, 2024 Order Modifying and Approving Temporary Variance of Article 405 establishes
a Van Cleef Lake target elevation of 428.5 feet Barge Canal Datum to address the reservoir-rim
dam-safety condition. The order also describes the New York Regional Office’s May 8, 2023
directive that the licensee was not authorized to raise the reservoir above the two-foot drawdown
without prior approval. The May 1, 2026 extension retains the earlier order’s requirements and
extends the variance through October 22, 2026.

The September report spreadsheet shows Van Cleef Lake maintained above 429 feet and near
429.3 feet during the latter part of the month, approximately 0.8 foot, or 9.6 inches, above the
stated variance target.

Since water is being released from Seneca Lake to maintain the level of Van Cleef Lake, the
discrepancy in the authorized level and actual level of Van Cleef Lake warrants an explanation of
the operating level being maintained and the releases necessary to sustain it. We request
information concerning approval authorizing the higher Van Cleef elevation, reconciliation with
the report’s claim of compliance with the variance, and an explanation of how releases were




                                                                          KleinschmidtGroup.com
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
November 9, 2026                                                                                  10.


limited to those necessary for applicable navigation, environmental flow, and dam-safety
requirements.

The Seneca Falls powerhouse has been offline since June. As such, all water received is passing
via Gate #4 and occasionally the spillway. While the initial 2± foot drawdown was conducted in
April 2023, and the FERC New York Regional Office (NYRO) provided feedback by letter dated
May 8, 2023 that C-S Canal Hydro LLC should not increase the elevation of Van Cleef Lake above
428.5 ft without NYRO approval, the 428.5 ft elevation proved untenable for various stakeholders.
Specifically, as communicated to the FERC NYRO via email dated June 1, 2023 “In addition to
those who reside around the impoundment, the Town of Seneca Falls is being impacted by not
being able to use their docks mounted on the side of the canal walls, there is a canal festival planned
June 30th through July 2nd for the community that will be impacted, a golf course is unable to
utilize water, and [an] industrial company [is] impacted due to process water restrictions.” NYSCC
also indicated that the lower elevations were causing impacts to navigation operations. The target
elevation for the Van Cleef impoundment has been targeted at slightly higher, 429± ft since June
2023. These slightly higher elevations, which vary with hydrologic inputs, have been
communicated to FERC NYRO monthly since that time.

Comment 3

Flow accounting and recurring leakage entries

We have concerns regarding quality control issues in both the August and September report
spreadsheets. Column M is noted to contain the leakage from the stuck Seneca Falls gate (started
in mid-July) instead of the normal Bypass Gate and Leakage flow at Waterloo the monthly
spreadsheets typically document. Both spreadsheets report zero flow for every quarter-hour
record during days 1–9, then changes to a constant 164 cfs beginning on day 10. Neither filing
explains the repeated nine-day zero pattern or reconciles the later 164-cfs entries with the
approximately 175-cfs leakage described in the report narrative.

       Response:

       The flows through the bypass via leakage (when the bypass Taintor gates are not open) is
       2 cfs. The leakage column in the spreadsheet contains the combined values for lock
       leakage, estimated at 15 cfs uncontrolled, and impoundment migration leakage of
       approximately 5 cfs. Turbine flows are actual generation flows or 8 cfs of leakage per unit
       when the units are not generating. The minimum flows required from the Waterloo
       Development (inclusive of the leakage flows indicated) are 100 cfs.

       The discrepancy regarding the leakage entry was a misunderstanding of the reporting
       column definition and has been corrected in the attached Excel files for July, August, and
       September. The column that combined lock leakage (15 cfs) and bypass flow (min 2 cfs)
       from the Waterloo development has mistakenly had the leakage from the downstream
       Seneca Falls development misaligned gate included as the total. The mistake made it



                                                                               KleinschmidtGroup.com
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
November 9, 2026                                                                               11.


       appear that there was an estimated 164 – 175 cfs flowing out of Waterloo as leakage, and
       therefore Seneca Lake, instead of the typical bypass and lock leakage of approximately 17
       cfs combined, but that is not representative of the actual conditions. The estimated 164 to
       175 cfs gate leakage at the Seneca Falls development has already been accounted for by
       the discharge from the upstream Waterloo development. Since Seneca Falls is downstream,
       and has not been generating power since June, all inflow to the Seneca Falls development
       has been passed through the misaligned gate, and any excess flow beyond the estimated
       164 to 175 cfs that the gate is passing is being passed over the dam. The 175 cfs leakage
       from the Seneca Falls development should not have been included in the Waterloo leakage
       column, and has been removed from all data files so the data now accurately reflects the
       total discharge from the Waterloo development.


In addition, Column O (Project Discharge) includes Column M in its total. Adding downstream
Seneca Falls leakage to upstream Waterloo releases does not represent a single Waterloo
discharge. Perhaps there should be a separate column for the Seneca Falls leakage.

We request the spreadsheet be corrected and documentation supporting the leakage estimates and
constant cylinder-gate and fish-bypass values.

       Response:

       The downstream Seneca Falls gate leakage has been removed from the Waterloo discharge
       total, see response to previous comment for explanation. The Excel spreadsheets have been
       corrected for July, August, and September and are included with this filing. Additionally,
       Column M has been separated into two columns, one for lock leakage, and one for the
       bypass flow.

We recognize the Commission’s September 28, 2026 direction that Gate 4 repairs occur after the
navigation season. We note the September report does not provide a Gate 4 repair schedule. Given
that as of October 12, Seneca Lake is below 444 feet, causing issues with shore wells drying up
and other harm, we would like to understand the repair schedule and justified interim operating
controls consistent with that direction.

       Response:

       Details regarding the gate repair are outside the scope of the monthly 405 deviation reports.
       Repairs to the gate are planned for the fall/winter 2026, and details are being submitted
       under separate cover.

These recurring discrepancies and other data quality issues within the spreadsheets raise concerns
about the quality-control procedures used to prepare and review the monthly filings. We request
that the Commission require Relevate Power and its reporting consultant, Kleinschmidt
Associates, to conduct a comprehensive review of the August and September reports and
supporting spreadsheets, submit corrected filings, and explain the procedures they will use to



                                                                            KleinschmidtGroup.com
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
November 9, 2026                                                                             12.


prevent recurrence. The review should reconcile the precipitation explanation, Van Cleef
operating elevation, development-specific flow accounting, and identify whether the corrections
change the reported compliance conclusions or explanation for Seneca Lake’s continuing decline.

       Response:

       The corrections do not change the reported compliance conclusions or the reason for
       Seneca Lake’s continuing decline in elevation. As discussed above, the minor error of
       mistakenly using a precipitation figure that shows a week’s worth of data instead of a
       month’s worth of data, does not change the fact that precipitation has been below average
       for the preceding three months, and continues to be significantly below average into
       October, effecting the elevation of Seneca Lake.

       Kleinschmidt Associates has been in touch with the station operator to confirm conditions,
       and will continue to do so prior to future reports. The data spreadsheets for July, August,
       and September have been revised to show the correct value for discharge at the Waterloo
       development, and column M has been split into two columns to show the difference
       between the lock leakage and bypass flows. The corrected value shows a 175 cfs reduction
       in flow out of Waterloo in the Total Discharge column for the months of July, August, and
       September.

Dear Secretary Reese,

Kleinschmidt Associates, on behalf of Relevate Power (Relevate) and C-S Canal Hydro LLC,
owner and licensee, respectively, for the Waterloo and Seneca Falls Project (FERC No.
2438) on the Seneca River in New York, is filing this Article 405 Deviation Report for the
month of September 2026.

September 2026 Article 405 Reporting

During the month of September 2026, the level of Seneca Lake was below the target
elevation. The precipitation received for the month of September was approximately 75%
- 125% of the normal precipitation expected for the area where the Seneca Falls Project
is located, and is a continuation of the trend of lower-than-average precipitation values
since June, when rainfall totals began to decline. Lower water levels are typical for this
time of year depending on precipitation, and are consistent with this time in 2025, 2022,
2020, and 2016. The ongoing trend of low precipitation over several months has brought
the elevation of Seneca Lake down naturally while, as required by License Article 405, C-
S Canal Hydro has discharged flows adequate to maintain the elevation of Van Cleef Lake,
and navigation flows, which the level of Seneca Lake is subordinate to.

The level of Seneca Lake is also affected by the input received from the upstream Keuka
Lake. A significant portion of inflows into Seneca Lake are provided via Keuka Lake at its
outlet in Dresden, NY. The Keuka Lake USGS Gage 04232482 shown in Attachment C
demonstrates that releases from the lake outlet have generally been consistently under
25 cfs.



                                                                                          KleinschmidtGroup.com
 Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
October 9, 2026                                                                              2.


Throughout the month of September 2026 the level of the Cayuga-Seneca Canal has been
in compliance with the requirement to be maintained no lower than 0.5 ft below the
Seneca Lake elevation.

Throughout September 2026, the level of Van Cleef Lake was maintained at approximately
429.2 ft. This is slightly higher than the target elevation range as established in the Order
Granting Temporary License Variance dated November 12, 2025, and extended to
October 22, 2026 by Order dated May 1, 2026 1 . As discussed in the email from the
Licensee to FERC NYRO dated June 1, 2023, the slightly higher elevation is necessary to
avoid impacts to docks owned by residents and the Town of Seneca Falls, a local golf
course, and an industrial facility that had process water restrictions imposed. NYSCC also
indicated that the lower elevation in Van Cleef was causing impacts to navigation
operations. The target elevation for Van Cleef Lake has been slightly higher, at
approximately 429± ft since June 2023.

In support of this report, C-S Canal Hydro provides the following attachments:

you have any questions or require additional information regarding this matter.

Good afternoon,

I am writing to inform you that the elevation of Seneca Falls Lake has continued to drop to a low elevation of approximately 445.2 ft.
Average inflows to the Cayuga-Seneca Canal have been approximately 300 cfs for the last 30 days. These lower water levels currently
being experienced at Seneca Falls Lake (below target levels) do typically occur during the summer period depending on precipitation.
The low levels currently being experienced are consistent with those experienced last year and in 2022 (see attached), as well as in
2020 and 2016. Precipitation in the vicinity of the Project is less than half of normal for the last 30 days or so (see attached).

The FERC License and Water Quality Certification for the Project requires Seneca Falls Lake to be maintained within 0.3 ft of 446.0 ft in
the summer. However, the elevation of Seneca Lake is subordinate to the maintenance of the water levels for navigation (Cayuga-
Seneca canal) and the minimum flow to sustain Van Cleef Lake, which is currently being maintained approximately 2 ft lower than its
minimum summer elevation of 430.25 ft as per the Article 405 temporary variance to address shoreline remediation needs.

The Cayuga-Seneca Canal has been in compliance with the requirement to be maintained no more than 0.5 ft lower than the Seneca
Falls Lake elevation during this time. The Seneca Falls powerhouse is off-line and has been for most of the summer. Flows of
approximately 175 cfs are currently discharged through Gate 4, which would otherwise be passed at the spillway, as well as the lock
system. The Waterloo powerhouse is intermittently operational to maintain elevations in Seneca Falls Lake and the Cayuga-Seneca
Canal, as well as provide flows needed to retain the elevation in Van Cleef Lake, and meet the required minimum flows of 100 cfs from
June through September.

Please let us know if you have any questions.

Thank you,

Good morning,

I am writing to inform you that the elevation of Seneca Falls Lake has been variable at the low elevation of 445.7 ft for approximately the
last 14 days and has been steadily below elevation 445.7 ft (at 445.6 ft) for approximately the last week. These lower water levels
currently being experienced at Seneca Falls Lake (below target levels) do typically occur during the summer period depending on
precipitation.

The FERC License and Water Quality Certification for the Project requires Seneca Falls Lake to be maintained within 0.3 ft of 446.0 ft in
the summer. However, the elevation of Seneca Lake is subordinate to the maintenance of the water levels for navigation (Cayuga-
Seneca canal) and the minimum flow to sustain Van Cleef Lake, which is currently being maintained approximately 2 ft lower than its
minimum summer elevation of 430.25 ft as per the Article 405 temporary variance to address shoreline remediation needs. The
Cayuga-Seneca Canal has been in compliance with the requirement to be maintained no more than 0.5 ft lower than the Seneca Falls
Lake elevation during this time. The Seneca Falls powerhouse is off-line and the Waterloo powerhouse is intermittently operational to
maintain elevations in Seneca Falls Lake and the Cayuga-Seneca Canal, as well as provide flows needed to retain the elevation in Van
Cleef Lake.

Please let us know if you have any questions.

Thank you,
